etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English hayle, haile, hail, hawel, haghil, haȝel, from Old English hæġl, hæġel, hagol (“hail”), from Proto-West Germanic *hagl, from Proto-Germanic *haglaz, of uncertain origin. Either from Proto-Indo-European *kagʰlos (“pebble”); or, from *ḱoḱló-, a reduplication of *ḱel- (“cold”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian Hail (“hail”), West Frisian heil (“hail”), Dutch hagel (“hail”), Low German Hagel (“hail”), German Hagel (“hail”), Danish hagl (“hail”), Swedish hagel (“hail”), Icelandic hagl (“hail”). Compare also Old Norse héla (“frost”). Doublet of haglaz.

Root-cognates outside of Germanic include Welsh caill (“testicle”), Breton kell (“testicle”), Lithuanian šešėlis (“shade, shadow”), Ancient Greek κάχληξ (kákhlēx, “pebble”), Albanian çakëll (“pebble”), Sanskrit शिशिर (śíśira, “cool, cold”).

definitions.definition: (meteorology, uncountable) Balls or pieces of ice falling as precipitation, often in connection with a thunderstorm.
(meteorology, countable) An occurrence of this type of precipitation; a hailstorm.
(countable, by extension) A rapid, intense barrage by a large number of projectiles or other objects.

quote.citation: 2019 February 27, Drachinifel, 40:01 from the start, in The Battle of Samar - Odds? What are those?‎[1], archived from the original on 3 November 2022:
quote.text: Their lack of good intelligence also meant that they vastly overestimated the size of their foes for far too long, hails of armor-piercing shells doing comparatively little damage compared to the high explosive that they should have been using.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English haylen, haulien, hawelien, from Old English hagolian, hagalian (“to hail”), from Proto-West Germanic *haglōn, from Proto-Germanic *haglōną (“to hail”), from the noun (see above). Cognate with Saterland Frisian hailje (“to hail”), West Frisian heilje (“to hail”), Dutch hagelen (“to hail”), German Low German hageln (“to hail”), German hageln (“to hail”), Danish hagle (“to hail”), Swedish hagla (“to hail”), Norwegian Nynorsk hagle, hagla (“to hail”), Faroese hegla (“to hail”), Icelandic hagla (“to hail”).

definitions.definition: (impersonal) To have hailstones fall from the sky.
To pour down in rapid succession.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English heil (“healthy, sound”), from Old Norse heill, from Proto-Germanic *hailaz (“whole, entire, healthy”). The verb is from Middle English heilen, itself from the adjective. Doublet of whole, hale, and heil.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To greet; give salutation to; salute.

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “Book I”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC, lines 249–252:
quote.text: […]  Farewel happy Fields / Where Joy for ever dwells: Hail horrours, hail / Infernal world, and thou profoundeſt Hell / Receive they new Poſſeſſor:  […]

definitions.definition: (transitive) To name; to designate; to call.

quote.citation: 1671, John Milton, “Samson Agonistes, […].”, in Paradise Regain’d. A Poem. In IV Books. To which is Added, Samson Agonistes, London:  […]  J[ohn] M[acock] for John Starkey […], →OCLC, page 28:
quote.text: Such a Son as all men hail'd me happy;

definitions.definition: (transitive, by extension, UK, Australia) To indicate, from a designated stop or otherwise, to the driver of a public transport vehicle that one wishes to board and travel on the vehicle, usually using hand signals such as waving.
(transitive) To call out loudly in order to gain the attention of.

quote.citation: 1995, Alanis Morissette (lyrics and music), “Hand In My Pocket”, in Jagged Little Pill:
quote.text: 'Cause I've got one hand in my pocket / And the other one is hailin' a taxi cab

definitions.definition: (transitive) To signal in order to initiate communication with.
(transitive) In the game of uppies and downies, to throw (the ball) repeatedly up and down at the goal location, in order to score a point.
(from) to originate (from), be native (to) or be based (in)
(archaic or poetic) An exclamation of respectful or reverent salutation, or, occasionally, of familiar greeting.
